251.s: Albert argues Billy Douglas was no copyist and had an original style, even in his arrangements, despite claims he copied Cuban Bennett or Jabbo Smith. Douglas arranged Liza.
251.q: Better do a little more talking, Dick, so... Yeah, yeah. Well, tell me about this piano and everything. Well, this is Lord Glenn. I guess Billy Douglas comes back on this. It's Dean Taylor. Yeah. It's Billy Douglas back in. And you can hear the drum back as Albert Fastmore.

930.t: Harry James's vibrato, ballads, and Trumpet Blues
930.s: Reaction to the George Simon quote, Conte Candoli on vibrato, the Harry James biography, ballads, and Tony Scodwell on the spirit of Harry.
930.q: Conte Candoli summed it up. Now the book that was written on Harry, Trumpet Blues I was interviewed by the author, God, for a week. When that book came out he called me and apologized. He says, “Fred, you’re the first individual I interviewed about Harry James that looked at him on a different…

1042.t: Woody Shaw, his compositions and his place in trumpet history
1042.s: Asked about his melodic originals, Vega talks about Woody Shaw's Sweet Love of Mine and calls Shaw the last great innovator of the trumpet, also praising Tim Hagans.
1042.q: See Woody’s the perfect example of that. Because Woody’s music was harmonically very intellectual. He included rhythmic elements from Brazil and as well as Afro- Caribbean rhythms and swing. And when he soloed he was applying harmonic concepts that were not really that closely related to trumpet.…

141.t: Buck Clayton, Basie records and first hearing Dizzy's band
141.s: He names Buck Clayton as a favorite trumpeter and recalls Willie Cook leading Dizzy's trumpets.
141.q: I didn’t hear the band at... Willie Cook was playing the lead trumpet, and they had a lot of good musicians, and... I just remember hearing that band, and taking a liking to it. I don’t know...

491.t: Remembering Freddie Hubbard and Art Farmer, master of the ballad
491.s: Golson recalls Hubbard and mourns Art Farmer, whose sound and intervals made him the greatest ballad player; he explains why ballads reveal a musician.
491.q: Yeah. We did so many things together, Freddie. We went on a tour of Japan, and he played like a crazy – a wonderful crazy man.

228.t: Freddie Webster's sound and Miles's debt to him
228.s: McLean describes Freddie Webster's sound as a big red ball and hears Miles absorbing it.
228.ch: Harlem youth, Monk and Bird, and Greensboro
228.q: I saw him play twice. I saw him play that Sunday. His sound was like a big red ball, if you could imagine a guy with a trumpet like you’d blow a bubble from a bubble gum. You see a huge, shiny, red, beautiful ball come out of the front of his horn. Beautiful sound. Different than Fats or anybody. I…

409.t: Harold Baker, Willie Cook and Clark Terry
409.s: Cootie praises Harold Baker, Willie Cook and Clark Terry, who he thought did not get a chance with Duke.
409.q: Well, he has a great sound. And he produces. That's what I likes about him, you know, that's what I like about him. He has a great, a real great sound on his horn. And he's a very fine musician, too.

379.s: Cheatham played five or six years in Bauza's band; he admired his lyric style.
379.q: He play (inaudible) in my band. He stay with my band about five, six years, play well. He's a hell of a Dixieland man. He's one of the best left. He was -- I used to admire Cheetam -- I used to hear Cheetam in the record. I told you about McKinley's Cottonpickers. He was the first trumpet player in…

18.s: He praises Jabbo Smith as a real jazz player he knew briefly.
18.ch: Early influences, Oliver date and trombone peers
18.q: I don't know how to compare them. But, the only thing I know I just loved his playing. And he played jazz. And I mean real jazz.

115.t: Favorite tenor, trumpet and bass players
115.s: He names Ben Webster, Lester Young, Roy Eldridge, Hot Lips Page and Blanton.
115.q: Just kidding along, and when he made the record, I was surprised. I said, 'You did the same thing you did in the bus,' one of those things.

86.t: Bunny Berigan compared with Harry James
86.s: They agree Berigan had warmth and soul that James lacked.
86.ch: Opinions on singers, promotion and originality
86.q: But you could still listen to him and listen to --

473.t: Red Allen's feeling, singing and peak with Fletcher Henderson
473.s: At Stanley Dance's suggestion Jones discusses trumpeters as they come up; he admired Red Allen's soulful, unique sound, finding him greatest with Fletcher Henderson and good with Luis Russell.
473.q: Yeah, he was like -- he didn't have to play strong and he didn't have to play a lot of chords, because he could play eight bars and take down and take up and play another eight bars, you know, and play it.

13.t: Freddie Webster and Hines's ear for talent
13.s: Webster in later years; talent passing through.
13.ch: Swing, singers, Ed Fox and recordings
13.q: When we got Freddie Webster, I think that's the same time we got Kansas.

79.t: Describing a player's style: Sleepy Tomlin and Shorty Baker
79.s: Dance asks how to describe unrecorded trumpeters. Thomas refuses to compare players but calls Hal (Shorty) Baker the greatest trumpet player he ever heard.
79.ch: The levee club and the St. Louis scene
79.q: Never. Somebody has got to get somebody. I figure that way. Now, to give you an idea of what I mean since you gave me that idea, it could have been near to Joe Smith. Because Joe Smith was a great trumpet player I think.
